extracted.intended_audience: War Department officials, contracting officers, judge advocates, surety companies, and contractors dealing with official bonds and suretyship
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and legal rules governing the form, sufficiency, acceptance, and administration of bonds and corporate sureties for the War Department (including procedural requirements under acts of Congress and Army Regulations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Bond for ordnance stores — double value requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The regulations governing the issue of ordnance stores to educational institutions require that the bond given to secure the safe-keeping of the stores shall be in double the value of the stores issued.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is legally acceptable to accept a bond in excess of double the value (the excess may cover future issues as well as stores already issued). (C. 942, Nov. 22, 1909)

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantial compliance vs. defect for bond amount
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the statute requires the bond shall be in double the value of the ordnance stores issued, a bond which lacks $20 of being double such value is defective; but a bond that lacked 55 cents of being double the value was held to be substantial compliance with the statute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small shortfalls may be treated as substantial compliance depending on amount and circumstances. (C. 950, Jan. 24, 1908; C. 1766, Jan. 5, 1905)

rubrics_metrics.name: Correct recitation of issued vs to-be-issued stores on bond
rubrics_metrics.description: If a bond recites that certain ordnance stores 'have been issued' but the bond was intended to cover stores not yet issued, the language should be changed to 'to be issued.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where the bond fails to state whether stores had been issued or were to be issued (space left blank), the omission may be waived. (C. 1828, Nov. 18, 1895; C. 1711, Oct. 17, 1906; C. 24272, Dec. 30, 1908)

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority to decide sufficiency of sureties (Secretary of War)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 1191, R.S., requires officers to give good and sufficient bonds 'in such sums as the Secretary of War may direct'; although the section does not explicitly vest in the Secretary the power to decide sufficiency of sureties, by implication he has that power as the official charged with passing upon bonds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Therefore the Secretary may legally accept security (corporate surety) companies as sureties on such bonds, analogous to acceptance for contractors' bonds. (P. 50, 118, Nov. 2, 1891)

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence required to show corporate officers' authority to execute bonds
rubrics_metrics.description: Where regulations require filing a copy of the record of selection and qualification of corporate officers and copies of by-laws authorizing certain officers to execute bonds, attaching a certificate signed by 'A, secretary' stating 'B is the president and A is the secretary duly elected and qualified' is not proper evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The facts should appear from certified copies of the corporate records rather than a secretary's certificate. Such defects may be waived by the War Department where the property's value is small (example: $113.97). (C. 1482, June 21, 1895; C. 7666, Aug. 26, 1909; C. 3946, Aug. 16 and 22, 1906)

rubrics_metrics.name: Corporate surety remains bound despite principal's failure to pay premiums
rubrics_metrics.description: A corporate surety continues to be bound by a bond notwithstanding the principal may fail to pay the company the premiums agreed upon; the United States is not a party to the contractual premium arrangement and is not affected by principal's failure to pay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An attempt by the surety to cancel the bond is without legal effect. Liability of the surety continues until contract is performed or damages for breach are paid. The United States will not decide when the contractor should discontinue premium payments. (C. 8553, July 5, 1900; C. 22571, Jan. 6, 1908; C. 12359, Apr. 7, 1902)

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority of corporate agent to bind surety company — notice of revocation
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a surety company has furnished the War Department with proper evidence of the authority of an agent to bind the company and has not given notice of revocation of that authority, the company will continue to be bound by acts of the agent under his authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to notify the Department of revocation means the Department may rely on prior evidence of authority. (C. 18002, Apr. 18, 1908)

rubrics_metrics.name: Periodic examination of official bonds and corporate sureties (Act Mar. 2, 1895)
rubrics_metrics.description: The act of March 2, 1895 requires official bonds to be examined at least once every two years to ascertain sufficiency of the sureties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For bonds on which a corporation is surety, compliance is sufficiently met if the corporation files periodically in the War Department the financial statement required by paragraph 574, Army Regulations (585 of 1910). (C. 2516, Aug. 12, 1896)

rubrics_metrics.name: Extending a bond to a new office requires formal corporate instrument
rubrics_metrics.description: To extend an existing official bond to cover a new office (e.g., promotion from captain to major), a mere letter from the surety company's superintendent expressing willingness is insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extension requires an instrument under the corporate seal identifying the bond and executed by officers authorized to bind the company. (C. 4424, Apr. 21, 1899)

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirements for foreign-corporation surety acceptance (appointment of process agent)
rubrics_metrics.description: Before a corporation incorporated in one State will be accepted as surety on the bond of a principal residing in another State or Territory, it must comply with section 2 of the act of Aug. 13, 1894: appoint a written power of attorney agent residing within the judicial district where suretyship is undertaken and file authenticated copies as required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Once an appointment of an agent has been made, it is not necessary to file subsequent appointments in the War Department; the appointment must be in the judicial district in which the principal resides or, if a corporation, has its principal place of business. Appointment of an agent only in D.C. is insufficient to comply for principals elsewhere. In places without 'judicial districts' (e.g., Philippines as argued), require filing evidence of local agent for service. (C. 3946, Oct. 12, 1905; C. 501, Oct. 16, 1894; C. 11618, Dec. 18, 1905; C. 13893, Jan. 3, 1903)

rubrics_metrics.name: Attorney General's power to require additional security is prospective only
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 4 of the act of Aug. 13, 1894 gives the Attorney General authority to require additional security if he deems a surety company insufficient, but that authority is prospective only.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It does not authorize the Government to require a new bond for work already done as a condition of being allowed to complete the work. (O. 23265, Feb. 16, 1909)

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of Aug. 13, 1894 on state qualification requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: The act relating to acceptance of corporate surety does not require compliance with any State laws or regulations a State may impose to qualify a foreign surety company to do business within the State; under the federal act the bond to the United States is valid even if the surety hasn't complied with State requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The federal acceptance may validate bonds notwithstanding noncompliance with State qualification laws. (C. 3604, Oct. 22, 1897; C. 29275, Dec. 11, 1911)

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability of Aug. 13, 1894 to foreign/performed abroad contracts
rubrics_metrics.description: The act of Aug. 13, 1894 (acceptance of corporate surety) does not apply to a contract made with a foreign contractor where the contract is to be made and performed in the foreign country; similarly it does not apply to contracts made and to be performed in the Philippine Islands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In such cases a foreign surety company may be accepted even if it hasn't qualified under that act. Under the Secretary of War's general authority, corporations doing business in the islands may be authorized as sole surety provided they have legal authority to act as surety (example: an incorporated bank). (C. 19164, Feb. 9, 1906; C. 13893, May 1, 1909; July 23, 1909)

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit on bonds relative to paid-up capital and collateral for excess (par. 585-2)
rubrics_metrics.description: War Department regulation: no surety company will be accepted which shall execute bonds in excess of 10 percent of its paid-up capital and surplus unless the company is secured as to such excess to the satisfaction of the head of the department by insurance or by deposit in pledge or conveyance in trust of property equal in value to such excess; requires report showing amount and character of such securities for bonds in excess of the 10% limit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collateral securities or counter-indemnity received from persons secured may be regarded as a deposit with the company in pledge within the meaning of the regulations; if sufficient as to character and amount, credit may be taken in the required report. (C. 11618, June 3, 1907)

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of Treasury Secretary inquiry and limitation (Act Mar. 23, 1910)
rubrics_metrics.description: The act of March 23, 1910 permits the Secretary of the Treasury to inquire into the solvency of an incorporated surety and 'may require that additional surety be given at any time by any principal when he deems such company no longer sufficient surety.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The statute does not vest the Secretary of the Treasury with express authority to determine amount or character of additional surety for bonds of another department; in absence of express language, those determinations rest with the Secretary of War for War Department bonds. The acts also do not authorize the Secretary of the Treasury to determine the character of the instrument by which a surety shall be bound or the amount for which each surety may be accepted in one instrument. (C. 27826, Feb. 9, 1911; Mar. 21, 1911; C. 29037, Nov. 18, 1911)
